claims: A shooting star is not a star.
A shooting star is a meteor.
Meteors are usually tiny specks of dust or rock from space.
Meteors burn up upon entering Earth's atmosphere at speeds between 11 km/s and 70 km/s.
Meteors appear as bright, momentary streaks of light.
Meteor streaks of light are caused by friction heating the surrounding air.
Roughly 48.5 tons of meteorites impact Earth daily.
Most meteorite impacts on Earth are unnoticed.
Meteors are fast, bright streaks often green, orange, or yellow.
Meteors last less than a second.
Unlike airplanes, meteors do not blink.
Meteors are usually faster than airplanes.
Meteors appear as solid lines rather than dashed, flickering lights.
Meteors can appear anywhere.
During a meteor shower, meteors often seem to radiate from a specific constellation.
Most meteors range in size from a grain of sand to a pebble.
Most meteors burn up completely 60-80 miles up in the atmosphere.
Most meteors never hit the ground.
The largest meteorite ever found is the Hoba meteorite in Namibia.
The Hoba meteorite weighs over 60 tons.
In most cases, if a meteorite lands on private property, it belongs to the landowner.
Up to 10 million meteors can be observed in a single night from the dark half of the Earth.
The Geminids are annual events in December.
The Perseids are annual events in August.
